title: The Italian Job
full_review:
A gang of professional thieves tries to outfox one of their own who double-crossed them in the high-octane caper flick, "The Italian Job" (Paramount). Revamping the 1969 Michael Caine-Noel Coward theft classic, director F. Gary Gray scores points with deftly orchestrated action sequences, but jettisons both character and story weight to create a formulaic shell-game of follow the stolen gold.

The bare-bones plot goes something like this: boy gets gold, boy loses gold, boy gets gold and girl. The boy, Charlie Croker (Mark Wahlberg) is a mastermind thief, the brains behind a motley crew of cons, each lending a talent to his scheme du jour. The purloining posse include veteran safecracker John Bridger (Donald Sutherland), inside man Steve (Edward Norton), computer hacker nonpareil Lyle (Seth Green), demolition expert Left-Ear (Mos Def) and English wheelman Handsome Rob (Jason Stratham).

Passing for the emotional impetus and raison d'etre for much of the high jinks is the father-son relationship shared by Croker and Bridger; one can almost imagine them playing catch in the prison yard. Prompted by the old yegg's advice to give up his thieving ways and settle down into an early retirement, Croker plans one last heist promising a payoff with a slightly higher yield than your typical 401(k). The swansong operation -- fleecing $32 million worth of gold bullions from a Venetian palazzo -- goes off without a hitch. However, after a clean getaway, one of the team betrays Croker, kills Bridger and makes off with the loot, leaving the rest for dead.

Having survived the traitor's treachery, Croker and his remaining merry men, bent on retrieving what is rightfully theirs -- well, not exactly rightfully -- and avenging Bridger's murder, track the turncoat and the gold to Los Angeles. The only problem is that the booty is snug and secure in the mother-of-all safes in a well-guarded Beverly Hills mansion.

Enter Stella (Charlize Theron), Bridger's beautiful daughter and a chip off the old safecracking block. And while Bridger's apple has fallen to the other side of the legal fence, the sweet smell of revenge clouds Stella's better judgment, paving the way for a rollercoaster of a payback.

The key to any heist film is the element of surprise and the filmmaker's ability to keep the audience guessing -- an increasingly difficult task given the plethora of similarly premised flicks. Gray, adroit at weaving the narrative through a thicket of plot twists, is somewhat of a con man himself, sharking viewers into a game of three-card monty in which nothing is under any of the cards. The thrill-ride choreography and seen-it-before "gotcha" plot devices are tricks up his sleeve, distracting viewers from the pre-worn plot and hand-me-down characterizations.

Since the players serve a secondary role to the elaborate schemes involved, little if any emotional development is required or attempted. The result is an ensemble of caricatures, making it difficult for viewers to invest anything in the characters beyond adrenaline.

What must not be lost in the equation is that, like many films of this genre, the heroes' hats are not white, but gray. Rooting interest is not between good and bad, but between bad thieves and good ones -- all crooks nonetheless. Unlike the merry men of Sherwood Forest, who stole from the rich to give to the poor, Croker's amiable rogues fleece others' pockets to line their own. Early on, Bridger gushingly confesses to the boys how proud he is that they can pull off such jobs without having to use guns -- as if their criminal actions are somehow ennobled by not compounding theft with violence. Monetary gain, however, only motivates the first crime. Re-stealing the gold is fueled by an even more dubious and less Christian motive -- revenge. And while Christians are known to harbor soft spots for good thieves, vengeance cannot be applauded, no matter how ingenious the mode of exacting it.

Due to a benign portrayal of theft, an implied sexual encounter, an instance of rough language, some profanities, and brief instances of violence, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
